Loungers, the West Country‑based café‑bar group, will open Fosforo Lounge, King Street in Stretford on Saturday 28th November 2026, creating around 30 new jobs for local people.. . Fosforo Lounge will be open all day, every day, serving breakfast, brunch, lunch, dinner and drinks, with dedicated kids’, gluten‑free and vegan menus. . The site on King Street has been transformed by the Loungers design team into a warm, eclectic ‘home from home’ – their signature style. Fosforo translates to matchstick and is a nod to Manchester-based painter LS Lowry’s ‘matchstick men’ style.. . Fosforo Lounge’s all‑day menu will cater for every taste, from hearty comfort food to healthier choices and indulgent treats. Performed by Seva and created with Far From The Norm, this new solo work is an unfiltered exploration of healing, identity, and the invisible legacies passed from one generation to the ne An intimate, evolving portrait unfolds as time folds and refolds, bringing past and present selves into dialogue. Through searing physicality and emotional clarity, the body confronts inherited patterns and begins to rewire itself, reclaiming power with fierce, embodied intention Sing Child Sing is a portrait of a man suspended between memory and possibility, anatomically rebuilding himself as he loosens the patterns that have shaped him. Sun 08 Nov 2026 12:00PM Aldridge Studio Tickets Sun 08 Nov 2026 3:00PM Aldridge Studio Tickets There is only one word used in our show - it’s ‘Hay!’ Like the stuffing in Geenie’s scarecrow, ‘Hay!’ like the sound she makes when he comes to life and ‘Hay!’ when he sees all the wonders of the natural world for the first time. Only one word but so many meanings in a show about growing up in the heart of the countryside and discovering that you don’t have to stay stuck in the mud – you can live your dreams, spread your wings and fly like the birds. A highly accessible show filled with music, clowning, song and dance. In this beautiful story Farmer Geenie guides scarecrow step by step as he finds his feet, then his hands, his voice, his legs and his love of song and dance in a story about the fun of growing up where everyday there’s something new to make you say ‘Hay!’ Our two very talented physical theatre performers are expert clowns and so our show doesn’t use any words – everything is told in a fantastically clear way through sound, dance, music and our incredibly inventive props which playfully represent the essential elements of nature that this show celebrates. We’ve got charming puppets – the birds of course and also the butterflies and bees - and some very wonderful eggs each with their own particular surprises. All of this means that our show is highly accessible and perfect for a younger age-group who will be giggling all the way through this gentle introduction to what theatre can be - sweet, funny, inclusive and uplifting. evidence_packet.evidence_text: Bolton Car Boot Sale is one of the North West's biggest weekly boot sales, held in the hardstanding car park of the Macron Stadium (formerly Reebok), Burnden Way, Horwich, Bolton BL6 6JW. It runs every Sunday from February right through to December, drawing over 300 sellers and thousands of bargain hunters each week. Sellers can arrive and set up from 6:00 AM, with buyers welcomed in from 7:00 AM. Entry costs just £1 per car for buyers. Pitches for sellers are £14 for a car, £20 for a van and £3 for a trailer, with regular and corner pitches available on request. Bring exact change to keep the queue moving, and call organiser Andrew on 07470784644 for more details. Expect hundreds of stalls across the concrete hardstanding pitches, so it goes ahead in most weather. On-site you'll find a 5-star catering service, doughnuts and coffee, ice cream and desserts, a meat auction, fresh fruit and veg, plants, and retro sweet stalls. The sale is dog-friendly, has male and female toilets, ample parking, and kids' rides and bouncy castles to keep little ones entertained. Last confirmed: 10 September 2026 Event date: 2026-11-08 Venue: Bolton Car Boot Sale Price: £1 Status: https://schema.org/EventScheduled

In August, Nothing Gold Can Stay took Robert Frost’s poem about transience as its starting point. Where that show dwelt on things passing, this one is more interested in what lasts The four contributing artists each approach time differently, thinking about how the past and the future shape the way ideas are understood. Anna Clough, a Cumbrian-born artist based at Salford’s Paradise Works, has made walking performances tracing mining landscapes from the Neo Sheffield’s Charlotte Dawson treats everyday objects – souvenirs, collections – as vessels for memory. Olivia England, who graduated from Manchester School of Art alongside Clough, reworks found objects, text and imagery through bookbinding and print, while London-based Elliot Fo Seeing the work from a perspective that isn’t your own is meant to open up conversations about the legacy of ideas, collective memory and what our actions leave behind for people we’ll never meet

evidence_packet.evidence_text: A neglected war memorial has been painstakingly restored by volunteers and lit up for the first time in its 104-year history ahead of Remembrance Day The Grade II* listed Hoylake and West Kirby monument has been transformed thanks to 14 years of renovations by the Friends of Grange Hill and Wirral Borough Council The spectacle is just one of a range of colourful tributes and events ahead of Remembrance Sunday across north-west England They include a striking display of thousands of poppies and crosses on a roundabout in Leigh, Greater Manchester, while Poulton-le-Fylde in Lancashire, has a displayed more than a 1,000 yellow poppies to honour "forgotten heroines" who served their country The Hoylake and West Kirby restoration project began in 2012 after a visitor tried to bring his father, a military veteran, to the memorial but found access virtually impossible Years of neglect had left the site overgrown while the site's remembrance garden had almost disappeared

evidence_packet.evidence_text: Manchester's Free Trade Hall has a special place in music history, as the venue - now a hotel - hosted some landmark moments It was where an electric guitar-wielding Bob Dylan famously faced an accusation of "Judas!" from a disgruntled folk fan , where a Sex Pistols show that inspired some of the city's most famous bands and the legendary Factory Records and where rock giants Kiss made their UK debut And it was where The Smiths, one of Manchester's most iconic bands, played what would prove to be their final farewell to the city on 30 October 1986 Forty years on, rarely-seen photos of the show, taken by then-student Alison Bell show what she said was a "dramatic" and "amazing" night Bell, who had been drawn to Manchester by its music scene as a student and went on to have a successful career in music promotion, said she had been desperate to see the band and the Free Trade Hall show was "the first opportunity I had to see them" Formed by singer Morrissey and guitarist Johnny Marr in 1982, the band were at the peak of their powers at the show, riding high on the success of their third long-player, The Queen Is Dead, which would go on to become widely-regarded as one of the greatest albums of all time

Manchester-based Crediflow AI automates the manual work that goes into preparing and assessing business loans, which limits how many deals lenders can take on and makes smaller loans to SMEs expensive to underwrite. The company has developed a platform that pulls together the information credit teams currently gather and process by hand, such as financial statements, bank transactions and borrower documents, and turns it into structured credit analysis. In practice, the platform extracts and standardises figures from a borrower’s accounts – a process the industry calls financial spreading – analyses cash flow and drafts the memo a lender’s credit committee uses to approve a loan, in each customer’s preferred format. The platform is already used by hundreds of credit professionals across the UK, Europe and the US, supporting lenders of all sizes, from specialist lenders such as AddWorking Capital to global captive finance such as Iveco Capital. Crediflow was founded by CEO Drey Kenfack, who has more than a decade of experience in commercial lending and private credit, including senior credit roles at Ford Credit Bank, DF Capital Bank and Advance Global Capital. The round was led by NPIF II – PXN Equity Finance, which is managed by PXN Ventures as part of the Northern Powerhouse Investment Fund II (NPIF II), with investment also coming from Haatch and angel investors. They labelled them a ‘backwards step’ for and an ‘unwelcome curtailing’ of democra Under the new rules planning applications would be split into two tiers – Schedule 1 applications and Schedule 2 applications, designated by planning officers. Schedule 1 includes smaller and more technical applications that would only be dealt with by planning officers Schedule 2 covers larger applications, which may be brought before the planning committee, if agreed by the planning committee chair and the council’s chief planning officer. The move also removes elected members’ right to ‘call in’ a planning application for scrutiny and debate The new rules came into force at the end of October, with Bury council now having approved the change in its constitution needed to meet the new legal requirements. Add to preferred sources Comments News Decla Dozens of extra enforcement and safety officers are being drafted in to keep Greater Manchester’s buses safe ahead of the launch of free bus passes for 11 to 16-year-olds in January Up to 200,000 young people will be able to apply for a bus pass when applications open on December 8, in a move which is expected to cost Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) up to £20m The pledge to give free bus travel for 11 to 16-year-olds was one of the first moves by Bev Craig after she was elected as Greater Manchester mayor. It builds on the Our Pass scheme, which was introduced in 2019 and offers free bus travel for 16 to 18-year-olds But at a scrutiny meeting on Wednesday (October 28), Councillor John Leech said it could cause ‘the potential for some disturbance’ on certain Bee Network routes Steve Warrener from TfGM said more travelsafe support and enforcement officers (TSEOs) are being brought in to manage the impact

The Salford Rise is a new bridge for pedestrians and bikes connecting Salford Uni The 11-metre wide and 220-metre long walkway in the sky crosses Frederick Road, featuring gardens, benches, and chill-out spaces overlooking the city’s rapidly changing skyline. The multi-million pound project, partly funded by the government’s £13.17m Levelling Up Fund, is remin The new bridge caused a stir in the neighbourhood throughout its two-year building period, with the busy thoroughfarer Frederick Road shut off for construction works for several months in 2024 and 2025, causing traffic and diversions Finalising the bridge for public use has also been straddled by some delays, with the fly-over originally due to open in the summer. Because of a number of ‘administrative hang-ups’, the ownership has not yet been transferred to the local council, with the route now due to open b Once open, works will begin on the Salford University campus walkways to ensure the bridge is fully accessible for wheelchair users

A consultation on the city-region’s first Bus Network Accessibility Plan starts next week which hopes to get a wide range of feedback how bus travel can be improved The draft plan states that several barriers to accessibility remain on the network These include access to bus stops, availability of passenger information, ease of boarding, availability of assistance and the consistency of facilities at Greater Manchester’s interchanges Recent changes to improve accessibility have included audio-visual announcements and next-stop screens on buses, hearing loops, high-contrast handrails and anti-slip flooring Newer buses also include two dedicated wheelchair spaces and room for an assistance dog close to its owner

evidence_packet.evidence_text: East Manchester Major road near Etihad Stadium to reopen eight MONTHS after giant hole appeared The busy stretch of road in east Manchester has been shut off for eight months after a historic mineshaft caused the road to collapse Add to preferred sour A stretch of one of Manchester’s busiest roads is to reopen after eight months of work fixing a giant hole. The northbound section of Alan Turing Way, in Beswick close to the Etihad Stadium , was shut off in March after a suspected sinkhole was discovered For months the council wasn’t entirely sure what had caused the stretch of road to collapse. But in September, engineers discovered it was a 50m-deep mineshaft under the road that triggered the 3m-wide crater There is a long history of mining and colliers throughout east Manchester, but this mineshaft wasn’t recorded on historic maps and took workers by surprise. Further investigations revealed the extent of the cavity and scale of repairs required In order to stabilise the shaft, contractors filled it with 120 tonnes of concrete grout before putting a ‘reinforced concrete slab’ over the top. Concrete has also been used to 'backfill' the original excavation with utilities pipes, and the road surface, then being restored In an update, Manchester City Council said the 'unprecedented' and 'highly complex' works were 'reaching their conclusion' and that the road would reopen on Saturday, November 28. It is expected to be clear by mid-morning

The rail firmed announced that around 70 additional Sunday services will return this winter following its landmark agreement with the RMT union, which comes ahead of a new timetable next The agreement between Northern and the RMT union brought to an end the the longest-running industrial dispute on the railway and paved the way for a phased return of Sunday services across the North West. Around 70 additional trains are expected to return each Sunday this winter, The additional services will be introduced over the coming weeks, with priority given to routes which have had little or no Sunday train service for more than two years, as well as supporting major events such as the region's Christmas markets. Alongside the Sunday service improv The changes are designed to improve punctuality, make better use of railway infrastructure and provide improved connections for customers. That depends who you ask… Tech by Chris Newbould November 4, 2026 Lecturers and students have significantly different perceptions of how much generative artificial intelligence (AI) is being used in university studies, according to new research from The University of Manchester and Spain’s Universidad del Pais Vasco/Euskal Herriko Unibertsitatea. The study found that academic staff perceived students to be using AI tools such as ChatGPT for their studies much more extensively than students reported themselves. Researchers say the findings highlight a gap in understanding between staff and students, at a time when universities are grappling with how best to respond to the technology. Academic staff rated their perception of students’ AI use at 5.23 out of seven, compared with an average of 3.11 among students reporting their own use for academic purposes.
